The scheduler retries a failed placement after a short delay and records that attempt in the audit log for the on-call engineer to review later. Retries are capped at five, after which the placement is parked and the queue depth metric rises so that the autoscaler reacts.

## Why retries

Retries absorb a transient failure without paging anyone, which keeps the rota quiet during a partial outage of the storage tier and avoids waking an engineer for a fault that resolves itself within a second or two of the first attempt failing. The cap is five, and beyond that the placement is parked for manual review the next morning by whoever picks up the queue, which in practice means the person already handling the incident.

Beyond that the placement is parked and the queue depth metric rises, which is what the autoscaler watches. We have not measured whether five is the right cap.

Compression cut the response size by about a third on the endpoints we sampled, though we did not isolate it from the index change that shipped the same week. The p99 numbers below come from the load test rather than production traffic, so treat them as a ceiling.

We ran the test twice. The second run used the same fixture set but a warm cache, which is closer to how the service behaves after a deploy has been live for an hour or so, and the difference between the two runs was smaller than the run-to-run variance we saw across a week of nightly builds.

The read path still dominates. Roughly four fifths of the sampled requests never touch the write queue at all, and of the remainder about half are retries of a request that already succeeded once, which suggests the client library is more eager than it needs to be.

Two open questions remain. Whether the index change alone accounts for the improvement, and whether the retry behaviour is worth fixing before the next release, both need someone to sit with the traces for an afternoon rather than another round of load testing.
